head: 6e341c27
gate: HTTP/2 continuous concurrent serving: spurious-timeout-free command/body waits and a lazily grown per-connection handler worker pool

commands.h3_concurrent: zig build test-lib -Dtest-filter="HTTP/3 continuous concurrent" --summary all
commands.handshake_bounded: zig build test-lib -Dtest-filter="handshake concurrent serving bounds" --summary all

benchmark.host: same host as the weft HTTP/1 reference; 32 logical CPUs

batch32.warning: one 'http2 response failed: Timeout' per run

notes: The server's ConcurrentStream.writeData waits on a command Event with no deadline. std.Io.Event.waitTimeout reports error.Timeout when a futex wait returns spuriously, even with .none, so a healthy write could surface Timeout, the handler reset the stream, and weft logged 'http2 response failed: Timeout'. The engines now loop on the event until it is set, or until the caller's absolute awake-clock deadline actually expires. Handlers previously ran one std.Thread per stream; a sequential request paid a spawn+join every time. The engines now use a per-connection worker pool that grows lazily while all workers are busy, up to max_streams. A sequential connection keeps one reusable worker; batch=32 grows to 32 workers. worker_stack_size defaults to 1 MiB. The new HTTP/2 stress test sends 100 batches of 32 streams (3200 requests) and asserts every response, exercising both the pool growth and the spurious-wake path. HTTP/3 uses the same pool. The HTTP/3 reader's availableDataBytes remains strict (UnexpectedFrame when no DATA frame is current, preserving the API-state test); the streaming engine treats that as 'no resident bytes' because the next data_available event carries the next frame. The unrelated pre-existing datagram pacing/QPACK feedback test fails on 73c34dac, 24d60aef and 6e341c27; it is not touched by these changes. The full unfiltered suite also shows intermittent failures in the MQTT outbound-bridge and WebSocket HTTP/1 handshake tests; the MQTT case still flaked with the new stress test removed, and both pass in isolation, so they are pre-existing timing-sensitive tests rather than regressions from the worker pool.
